sentences.text: 19. On perusal of examination-in-chief by way of affidavit of PW-1, it is noted that PW-1/Victim/Injured/Petitioner deposed on the lines of petitioner's original stand as already noted above.
It was further deposed that due to rash and negligent driving of the R-1, the accident in question took place.
20. Such witness was cross-examined by learned counsel for R-1 & R-2.
During cross-examination of PW-1 by learned counsel for insurance company, he deposed that at one point of time, two big vehicles can ply on the road where the accident took place.
He further explained that he was in the right lane of the road.
He further denied suggestion that accident took place due to his own rash and negligent driving.

But he admitted that offending vehicle came from behind therefore,he cannot tell the speed of the vehicle, although he admitted that in his examination in chief by way of affidavit, para-3 he deposed that such offending vehicle came at a fast speed.
Further, during his cross-examination by learned counsel for R-1, such PW-1 deposed and admitted that he did not tell the speed of offending vehicle at the time of accident.
He denied the suggestion that left side of the road is to be used by motorcycle as per MV Act.
Instead he stated that two wheeler can run on any side of the road.
He further denied the suggestion that the was trying to overtake the car by high speed and in a zig- zag manner.
He further denied the suggestion that due to pothole in the road, he fell down from the motorcycle.

He denied the MACT No.: 852/17 Satish Kumar v. Poonam Mittal Page No. 6 of 26 BK suggestion that car of R-1 did not hit the motorcycle of such injured.
21.

On the other hand, it is deposed by driver of such alleged offending vehicle, Ms. Poonam Mittal in her examination in chief by way of affidavit, her vehicle is not involved in the accident, she further deposed that it was learnt that injured/claimed was under the influence of alcohol and was illegally driving the vehicle on road.
She further deposed that accident was caused by some other vehicle.
She further deposed that she was diligently and properly driving the car and did not make any mistake or error.
22. Such R-1W-1/driver of alleged offending vehicle was cross-examined by claimant.
During such cross-examination, she admitted that she was driving the offending vehicle at the time of accident.

4
She further admitted that criminal case trial is pending before concerned learned Magistrate.
She further admitted that she has not filed any separate complaint to any authority disputing the accident allegedly committed by her.
But she denied the suggestion that accident was caused due to her rash and negligent driving.
23. Thus there are two conflicting versions in the present case.
24. As per the case of claimant, due to rash and negligent driving of R-1, the accident in question took place.
Whereas as per the claim of respondent no.1, offending vehicle is not involved in the accident.
It is further claimed that due to fault of injured himself, he met with such accident.
25. In this case, it is not in dispute that R-1 was driving the offending vehicle in question at the time of accident.
Further, her MACT No.: 852/17 Satish Kumar v. Poonam Mittal Page No. 7 of 26 BK presence at the spot of accident is not disputed.
In fact, it is her own admission that she did not fled from the spot of the accident meaning thereby, she was present there in any case.
Thus, the moot question remain same whether such R-1 caused the accident in question by rash and negligent driving or not.

26. In the present case, although, the driver of the offending vehicle entered into a witness box, but the fact also remains that not only a charge sheet is filed against him but even cognizance for the offence u/s 279 and 338 IPC is taken against her by the concerned MM Court.
Further, she herself admitted that she did not file any complaint to any authority disputing the accident committed by her.
Further, from reading of reply of such R-1 and her evidence, there is improvement in the stand taken by such R-1.
In the reply, para-4 stand taken by such R-1 was that due to negligence of such claimant/injured himself, as he could not control his vehicle, he fell down on the road and sustained injuries.
Whereas, at the time of evidence, further stand taken by R-1 by putting suggestion such claimant that due to pothole on the road, he fell down.
Further, another suggestion/stand taken that such accident was caused by some other vehicle.
Furthermore, no convincing evidence placed on record, despite stand so taken by R-1, injured was under the influence of liquor.

27. Thus, having regard to the parameters of standard of proof in the case of present nature, a chargesheet filed against such R- 1 and the evidence proved on record, it is held that accident in question is caused due to rash and negligent driving of R-1.
28.
Accordingly, the issue No.1 is decided accordingly, in favour of the petitioner.

The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life,
his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

30. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, MACT No.: 852/17 Satish Kumar v. Poonam Mittal Page No. 9 of 26 BK medicines, transportation, nourishing food,
and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non -pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).

(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
30.1.

In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv).

30.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.

What requires to be assessed by the Tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured; and after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of a percentage of the income, it has to be quantified in terms of money, to arrive at the future loss of earnings (by applying the standard multiplier method used to determine loss of dependency).

32. Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and, if so,
the extent of such permanent disability.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.

After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.

Geological Survey of India, (2003) 3 SCC 148, the following was held while interpreting section 171 of the MV Act, 1988:-
Three decisions were cited before us by Mr. A. P. Mohanty, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant, in support of his contentions.

sentences.text: No ratio has been laid down in any of the decisions in regard to the rate of interest and the rate of interest was awarded on the amount of compensation as a matter of judicial discretion.

The rate of interest must be just and reasonable depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case and taking all relevant factors including inflation, change of economy,
policy being adopted by Reserve Bank of India from time to time, how long the case is pending, permanent injuries suffered by the victim, enormity of suffering, loss of future income, loss of enjoyment of life etc. into consideration.
No rate of interest is fixed under Section 171 of the MV Act 1988.
Varying rates of interest are being awarded by Tribunals, High Courts and the Supreme Court.
Interest can be granted even if a claimant does not specifically plead for the same as it is consequential in the eye of the law.
Interest is compensation for forbearance or detention of money and that interest being awarded to a party only for being kept out of the money which ought to have been paid to him.
No principle could be deduced nor can any rate of interest be fixed to have a general application in motor accident provision under Section 171 giving discretion to the Tribunal in such matter.

In other matters,
awarding of interest depends upon the statutory provisions mercantile usage and doctrine of equity.
Neither Sec. 34 CPC nor Sec. 4-A(3) of Workmen's Compensation Act are applicable in the matter of fixing are of interest in a claim under the Motor Vehicles Act.
The courts have awarded the interest at different rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

Therefore, in my opinion, there cannot be any hard and fast rule MACT No.: 852/17 Satish Kumar v. Poonam Mittal Page No.
